misconceptions.label: Current gets used up
misconceptions.description: Student believes current is consumed by a bulb or resistor, so less current leaves than enters.
telltale_phrases: the bulb uses up the current
current is consumed by the resistor
bulb mein current kha jaata hai
current kam ho jaata hai bulb ke baad
current khatam ho jata hai
misconceptions.correction: Current is the flow of charge and charge is not used up; the same current leaves a bulb as enters it. What the bulb uses is energy.
misconceptions.analogy: Water pipe through a water-wheel: same amount of water flows out; the wheel only takes energy from it.

misconceptions.label: Battery gives fixed current
misconceptions.description: Student thinks a battery supplies the same current no matter what is connected.
telltale_phrases: battery always gives the same current
current is fixed by the cell
battery se hamesha utna hi current aata hai
misconceptions.correction: A cell fixes the voltage, not the current. Current = V/R, so it changes when the resistance of the circuit changes.
misconceptions.analogy: A water tank gives fixed pressure; the flow depends on how narrow the pipe is.

misconceptions.label: More parallel resistors = more resistance
misconceptions.description: Student believes adding resistors in parallel increases the total resistance.
telltale_phrases: more resistors means more resistance
parallel adds up resistance
resistance badh jaayega kyunki aur resistor lage hain
total resistance sum hoga
misconceptions.correction: Each new parallel branch gives current one more path, so the total resistance goes down and is always less than the smallest branch.
misconceptions.analogy: Opening extra billing counters in a shop makes it easier, not harder, for the queue to move.

misconceptions.label: Voltage flows like current
misconceptions.description: Student treats voltage as something that flows through the wire, rather than a difference across two points.
telltale_phrases: voltage flows through the wire
voltage passes through the bulb
voltage bahta hai wire mein
voltage bulb ke through jaata hai
misconceptions.correction: Potential difference is measured across two points; charge flows, voltage does not. Voltage is the push, current is the flow.
misconceptions.analogy: Height difference of a waterfall is not the water itself; it is what makes the water flow.

misconceptions.label: Resistance depends only on material
misconceptions.description: Student thinks resistance depends only on the material and ignores length and cross-section area.
telltale_phrases: resistance depends only on material
length does not matter
copper hai to resistance same rahega
thickness se kuch farak nahi padta
misconceptions.correction: R = ρl/A. Resistance increases with length and decreases with area; the material only sets ρ.
misconceptions.analogy: A long narrow corridor is harder to walk through in a crowd than a short wide one, though the floor is the same.

misconceptions.label: Higher wattage always brighter
misconceptions.description: Student believes a higher-wattage bulb always glows brighter, even in series.
telltale_phrases: 100 W bulb is always brighter
more watt means more bright
jyada watt wala hamesha tej jalega
series mein bhi 100W zyada chamkega
misconceptions.correction: A bulb's rating is for its rated voltage. In series the same current flows, so the bulb with larger resistance (the lower-wattage one) glows brighter, since P = I²R.
misconceptions.analogy: A strong runner in a relay still must carry the same baton at the same pace as the others.

misconceptions.label: Ohmic resistance changes with voltage
misconceptions.description: Student thinks the resistance of an ohmic conductor increases or decreases when the applied voltage changes.
telltale_phrases: more voltage means more resistance
resistance increases as V increases
voltage badhane se resistance badh jaata hai
misconceptions.correction: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, V/I is constant, so resistance stays the same. Doubling V doubles I.
misconceptions.analogy: A straight road keeps the same width however fast cars drive on it.

misconceptions.label: Image type confusion in mirrors
misconceptions.description: Student thinks all mirror images are virtual or that images formed behind a mirror are real.
telltale_phrases: all images in a mirror are virtual
image behind the mirror is real
mirror ki image hamesha virtual hoti hai
peeche banne wali image real hoti hai
misconceptions.correction: A real image forms where rays actually meet and can be caught on a screen; a virtual image forms behind the mirror where rays only appear to meet. A concave mirror can form both.
misconceptions.analogy: A real image is like a projector picture on a wall; a virtual image is like the 'person' you see behind a bathroom mirror.

misconceptions.label: Ignoring sign convention
misconceptions.description: Student ignores the Cartesian sign convention, e.g. takes the focal length of a concave mirror as positive or uses object distance as positive.
telltale_phrases: focal length is always positive
I just put the numbers in
u ko positive le liya
sign ki zaroorat nahi, bas values daal di
misconceptions.correction: Distances are measured from the pole in the direction of incident light as positive. For a concave mirror, f and u are negative; for a convex mirror, f is positive.
misconceptions.analogy: Like a number line: left of zero and right of zero are opposite directions, so they need opposite signs.

misconceptions.label: Light speeds up in denser medium
misconceptions.description: Student believes light travels faster in a denser (higher refractive index) medium.
telltale_phrases: light moves faster in glass
denser means faster
ghane medium mein light tez chalti hai
glass mein speed badh jaati hai
misconceptions.correction: Light slows down in a denser medium since n = c/v; higher n means lower speed v.
misconceptions.analogy: Running on a road versus wading through mud: the thicker the medium, the slower you go.

misconceptions.label: Covering half a lens halves the image
misconceptions.description: Student thinks covering half the lens removes half the image.
telltale_phrases: half the image will vanish
cover half the lens and half the picture goes
aadha lens dhakne se aadhi image gayab
misconceptions.correction: Every part of a lens forms the complete image; covering half only makes the image dimmer, not incomplete.
misconceptions.analogy: Cutting a window pane in half does not remove half of the view; it only lets in less light.

misconceptions.label: Longer focal length = more power
misconceptions.description: Student believes a lens with a longer focal length is more powerful.
telltale_phrases: longer focal length means more power
bigger f, bigger power
focal length zyada hai to power zyada
misconceptions.correction: Power P = 1/f (f in metres). A short focal length bends light strongly, so it means high power.
misconceptions.analogy: A sharp turn changes direction more strongly than a gentle curve.

misconceptions.label: Myopia needs convex lens
misconceptions.description: Student thinks short-sightedness is corrected with a convex lens.
telltale_phrases: myopia is corrected by convex lens
nearsighted ko convex lens lagta hai
myopia mein convex lens use hota hai
misconceptions.correction: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina, so a concave (diverging) lens is used to push the image back onto it. Convex lenses correct hypermetropia.
misconceptions.analogy: If the picture lands too early, you need to spread the rays a little first.

misconceptions.label: Prism adds colours
misconceptions.description: Student thinks the prism creates or adds colours to white light.
telltale_phrases: prism adds colours to light
prism rang daalta hai
glass colours ko paida karta hai
misconceptions.correction: White light already contains all colours; a prism only separates them because each colour bends by a different amount.
misconceptions.analogy: A prism is like a sorting machine, not a paint box.

misconceptions.label: Wrong reason for blue sky
misconceptions.description: Student thinks the sky is blue because it reflects the sea, or that red light scatters the most.
telltale_phrases: sky is blue because of the ocean
sea ka reflection hai
red light scatters the most
laal rang sabse zyada bikharta hai
misconceptions.correction: Air molecules scatter short wavelengths (blue) far more than long ones (red), so scattered blue light reaches us from all directions.
misconceptions.analogy: Tiny ripples scatter small waves more than big ones.

misconceptions.label: Field lines can intersect
misconceptions.description: Student thinks magnetic field lines can cross each other.
telltale_phrases: field lines cross at the centre
lines can intersect
field lines ek dusre ko kaat sakti hain
misconceptions.correction: Two field lines would give two directions of the field at the crossing point, which is impossible, so field lines never intersect.
misconceptions.analogy: Two road signs pointing in different directions at the same spot would leave the driver confused, so a single spot has only one direction.

misconceptions.label: Only magnets make magnetic fields
misconceptions.description: Student believes only magnets can produce magnetic fields, not electric currents.
telltale_phrases: only magnets have magnetic fields
a wire cannot have a magnetic field
sirf magnet se field banti hai
taar mein se field nahi nikalti
misconceptions.correction: Oersted showed that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it, which is why a compass needle deflects near it.
misconceptions.analogy: A moving crowd of charges makes a 'wind' of magnetism around the wire, just as a moving fan makes air movement.

misconceptions.label: Force is along the field
misconceptions.description: Student believes the force on a current-carrying conductor acts along the direction of the magnetic field.
telltale_phrases: force is in the direction of the field
force along B
force field ki direction mein lagta hai
force B ke saath saath hota hai
misconceptions.correction: The force is perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field. Use Fleming's left-hand rule: Force, Field, Current are mutually perpendicular.
misconceptions.analogy: Like pushing a door sideways with your thumb even though the hinge line and your palm point elsewhere.

misconceptions.label: Earth wire / fuse confusion
misconceptions.description: Student thinks the earth wire normally carries current, or that the fuse goes in the neutral wire.
telltale_phrases: earth wire carries current
fuse goes in neutral wire
earth wire se current bahta hai
fuse neutral mein lagta hai
misconceptions.correction: The earth wire carries current only if there is a fault, to protect us from shocks. A fuse is put in the live wire so the circuit breaks before the appliance gets damaged.
misconceptions.analogy: Earth wire is the emergency exit that stays empty until a fire; the fuse is the main gate that closes at the entrance.

misconceptions.label: Angles measured from the surface
misconceptions.description: Student measures the angle of incidence/reflection from the mirror surface instead of from the normal.
telltale_phrases: angle between ray and mirror
i measured from the mirror surface
mirror se angle naapa
surface se angle liya
misconceptions.correction: Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured from the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface), not from the surface.
misconceptions.analogy: Like measuring how far you swing from a straight-up pole, not from the ground.

misconceptions.label: Formula used upside-down
misconceptions.description: Student rearranges or applies a formula the wrong way round, e.g. Q = I/t instead of Q = I × t, or V = R/I.
telltale_phrases: charge = current / time
Q = I / t
charge equals current divided by time
current ko time se divide kiya
V = R / I
I = Q × t
formula ulta laga diya
misconceptions.correction: Q = I × t: charge is current multiplied by time. Check the units: ampere × second = coulomb, while ampere ÷ second is not charge.
misconceptions.analogy: Distance = speed × time. You would never divide speed by time to find how far you have travelled.

misconceptions.label: Unit or prefix not converted
misconceptions.description: Student forgets to convert units or prefixes (mA to A, cm to m, minutes to seconds) before using a formula.
telltale_phrases: did not convert cm to m
forgot to convert units
mA ko A nahi kiya
cm ko m mein nahi badla
minutes ko seconds nahi kiya
units convert nahi kiye
milliamp
misconceptions.correction: Convert everything to SI units first: 1 mA = 0.001 A, 100 cm = 1 m, 1 min = 60 s. Then check that the unit of your answer matches the quantity you wanted.
misconceptions.analogy: You cannot add 2 rupees and 50 paise as '52'; first turn both into the same unit.

misconceptions.label: Other / unclear reasoning
misconceptions.description: Wrong answer that does not match a known misconception. The classifier must still give a short specific label and a targeted explanation.
misconceptions.correction: Let's go back to the basic definition and work it through step by step.
